6.t: EDITORIAL
The greatest event of the Current Year was of course The Jubilee. The 50th
anniversary of the founding of Wah Yan College, Hong Kong, was celebrated in mid-
December with a week of special events in the school and elsewhere. On the actual
anniversary date, 16th, there was a special thanksgiving Mass in the School chapel
conceleprated by H.E. Bishop Hsu with four former students （including Fr. Joseph Tal）
and four rectors, past and present. Mass was followed by an invitation dinner in the
sChool hall at which every facet of Wan Yan's fifty years was representea-past and
present teachers, old boys, student associations, the domestic staff, present pupils，
Eaucation Department officiais, the very first student entered on the roll in 1919, and in
places of honour the founder of the college, Mr. Peter Tsui and his wife. Mr. Tsuli, a
sprigntly 82, treatea the nearly 300 guests to a charmingly simple and witty speech
when it came to his turn at the microphone. But this was not the only occasion that
week when the history of fifty years was rehearsed. Speech Day was held on the 19th，
and in the Queen's Theatre that morning. Mr. Tsui was greeted by thunderous and
prolonged applause from the assembled students, whom he addressed on the occasion.
Mrs. Tsul, assisted by her daughter, Mrs. Agnes Ng of the present Wah Yan staff，
distributed the prizes and certificates. A distinguished guest at the function and at the
Jubilee dinner that evening in the Ying King restaurant was Bishop Ratna of Ratcha-
bur'， Thailand, a Wah Yan （and Ricci） past student who had arrived with two other
past students from Thailand the previous evening. Their presence was unexpected, but
the pleasure of their company more enjoyable for that. Bishop Hsu, who had taught
Sports Day which this year formed part of the Jubilee celebrations. An Open Day was
neld on Sunday 14th, for which students and members of scnool Clubs and societies
put in a lot of work decorating the school and mounting various displays in the class-
rooms. The final Jubilee event was a grant ball in the Hiton Hotel on the 23rd, at-
tended by about 400 past pupils and their wives, financees or friends.
To mark the Jubilee, three new perpetual scholarships have been established in
the college, named for Mr. Peter Tsui, Mr. Cromwell Hall （a former Union president
who died earlier in the year） and Mr. Ho Sai Chue, as well as a Lim Hoy Lan Memorial
Award in Chinese studies （Mr. Lim was headmaster when the Society of Jesus took
over the management of Wah Yan）.
Those who came to celebrate the Jubilee with us were many. Two former
Rectors of the College Fathers E. Bourke and A. Cooney came from Malaysia. Also Fr.
Grogan, a former Prefect of Studies, returned to take up residence in the College.

7.t: The Student Council continues to play an important part in the life of the
school. Representatives from Form 2 now attend the meetings and also the House
Captains. Meetings are held every fortnight. The Council organises the Dramatic
Competition and Teachers' Day as well as a number of the events of the Jubilee
Celebration including the Open Day and the Students' Jubilee Concert.
Students have been very active during the year in sports and extracurricular
activities organised by various school clubs and societies. Events like the Talent
Time have been great attractions to the students. The Christian Life Community，
the Crusaders of the Blessed Sacrament and the Altar Society continue to work
much for the spiritual life of the school. All these help to develop a sound and
upright character. The school has always tried to train the students both physically
and mentally. And here the students give a great response. The pages that follow
are sufficient proof.

32.t: Mr. Peter Tsui Yan Sau
FOUNDER OF WAH YAN
R aer T auh Yen Sau ross Born in ihe Disrict of Ne Wah. Kwangtuing Province，
China, in the year 1889. He was the son of Mr. Tsui To Leung, a Protestant
minister. He ranks seventh in a family of nine children, three boys and six girls. Two
of his sisters are still living.
As a young boy, he came to Hong Kong and studied in St. Joseph's college.
It
was here that he received the Catholic faith. Besides having been a teacher in his alma
mater, he also taught in Ying Wah College and in a middle school in Mui Hsien.
Single-handed, Mr. Tsui founded Wah Yan School on December 16, 1919 at No.
60 Hollywood Road, second and third Floor. He started with an extremely meagre
number of four pupils. However, boys began to pour in and by the following year the
number on roll became so large that he had to turn his residence No. 33 Mosque Junction
into two classrooms. In 1921 the school moved to No. 2 Robinson Road. The school
expanded both in quality and size. This caught the notice of the then Education Depart-
ment, and the government offered to make Wah Yan into a Grant-in-Aid school, beginning
from October 1, 1922. Such a move created history in Hong Kong for never before
was a private school managed by a Chinese individual made into a Grant-in-Aid school.
The day on which Wah Yan turned into a Grant-in-Aid school was memorable for an-
other reason, for on that same day Mr. Lim Hoy Lan, who later became the head-master
of the school and whose energetic leadership made the school what it was, joined the
teaching staff.
The Kowloon branch started at Portland Street in 1925 and moved to
the new building at Nelson Street four years later.
Mr. Tsui paid his teachers well. Indeed, his teachers were better paid than the
Chinese teachers in government schools.
It was because of this that the government
started to revise the scale of the teachers' salary. During his time also, lady teachers
received equal pay with their men colleagues.
By 1933, the school had been handed over to the Jesuit Fathers.

33.t: Mr. Lim Hoy Lan
OR so many Wah Yan Old Boys in Hong Kong and in Kowloon for more than
thirty years the mention of the old school inevitably recalls the image of Mr. Lim
Hoy Lan. On formal and respectful occasions, they spoke of him as Headmaster Lim；
on less formal and more familiar ones, everybody knew him as Tiger Lim. A man severe
he was, and stern to view
..•Goldsmith's Village Schoolmaster certainly had not Mr.
Lim's charm and smile, but nevertheless Mr. Lim was a firm ruler of his student body.
One of Hong Kong's greatest schoolmasters, he is remembered with affection by literally
thousands of boys.
And after all that is the test: not how popular he was with the
current students but ten years or so after they had left his charge.
It is part of Mr. Peter Tsui's genlus that he was determined to have Mr. Lim Hoy
Lan with him when he launched his English school for Chinese boys, and have him he
did.
He persuaded Mr. Lim tn leave St. Joseph's and to join him in Robinson Road. It
may have been the clash of two very vigorous personalities that caused Mr. Lim to
tender his resignation later. Nr. Tsui would not hear of it, talked him out of it, and
instead, stepped down and made Mr. Lim headmaster in his place. The years rolled on.
Mr. Tsui was “Correspondent” and Mr. Lim ran the school in Robinson Road. Later
after it had been put under the care of the Jesuit Fathers, he crossed over to Kowloon
and took command of the Branch School in Nelson Street. And perhaps it is been that
one comes across more potent reminders of his personality. Til today, just inside the
main entrance hangs the chart showing the_ right and the wrong way to hold a pen，
something perhaps very unusual when Mr. Lim began his teaching; the brush was more
familiar to Chinese boys. Such a chart echoed Mr. Lim's meticulous care for detail, the
care which made him an excellent teacher of grammar and composition, the same care
which made him go over all the lesson books of his own children at the beginning of
each school year, carefully writing in helpful notes in the margin. No doubt about it he
was a born schoolmaster; he could scarcely have been anything else. And still he was a
competent and efficient administrator as well，-all with that easy. smile that welcomed
new teachers of another race and gave them those Kindly helpful hints that would make
their work easier and more successful.

38.t: A Short History of Wah Yan
1919 Wah Yan College was born in December at No. 60 Hollywood Road.
Ihe school moved to new premises, in Robinson Road.
Owing to the increase in applications for admission a branch school was
opened in Portland Street,Kowloon.
The Kowloon branch school moved to Nelson Street.
The College was transferred to the care of the Society of Jesus on 22nd
December. The late Fr. R. W. Gallagher, S. J. was the first Rector.
A branch for Senior students was opened on 8th September in Austin
Road, while Junior Classes continued in Nelson Street, under Mr. Lim
Hoy Lan. Austin Road had a short life as it closed on 9th December，
the day after the Japanese invasion.
Wah Yan College re-opened on 8th September. Later in the year a
Chinese stream （Wah Yan Middle School） was added.
In March the organisation of the Wah Yan Dramatic Society commenced.
The first production was “The Thrice Promised Bride”， performed in
the French Convent Theatre. The Society was formally established in
On 8th September the school at Nelson Street re-opened, with 560 pupils
on the roll.
The Boys' Club was opened on 15th November, with 19 boys. Mr.
Joseph Cheung helped at the beginning and is still with the Club.
1948 The Night School was started on 17th Feoruary.
1949 An afternoon school opened, with more than 700 boys enrolled.
On 10th October the site for the new College in Waterloo Road was
blessed.
The Chinese Section of the school was closed down.
The Governor，
Sir Alexander Grantham, opened Wah Yan College，
Kowloon, on 12th December.
The Afternoon School in Wah Yan, Hong Kong, closed.
On 7th October the foundation stone of Wah Yan College, Queen's Road
East, was blessed and laid.
Formal opening of Wah Yan College, Queen's Road East, was performed
on 27th September by His Excellency the Governor, Sir Alexander
Grantham.

70.t: In Memory of A Late Classmate
LUI WING TAT
On the fourth day of the School Certificate Examination Lui Wing Tat was taken
to hospital because he had a great fever. On the following day he passed away of blood
cancer. It was Sunday, May 24th. We were about to visit him when we were told that he
had already died.
We could hardly believe it; it was so sudden. The memory of Ah Tat，
as we used to call him, is still very vivid in our minds.
As a young man of seventeen, Ah Tat had a very strong character.
Once he had
made up his mind he seldom gave in. He was honest, sincere, friendly, and gentle. One
thing we can never forget is that he never let his friends down.
• He did his very best in
helping others. When he saw something wrong he always spoke out against it without
fear. He was very straightforward. We never heard him swear and he never grumbled.
He was humble, and always expressed disgust towards people who wanted to attract atten-
tion. He hated dirty jokes.
As a Wah Yan student for five years, Ah Tat had always been a conscientious one.
He iiked chemistry and biology very much. He was among the top boys in class. He liked
talking and often made the teachers his butt. He liked helping others in their studies.
He loved folk songs. He was the vocalist of the folk group called ‘The Turn' who
came first in the Talent Time 1969. He was a lover of sports. He liked football and won
the B Grade shot-put and hign-jump championshups. He also represented the school in
many occasions. Once he took part to represent the school in a Judo Tournament against
Salesian School.
Although Ah Tat had died, those who knew him will remember him as an ordinary
young man who had lived a meaningful life.

146.t: FROM OUR STUDENTS
ARRIVING IN HONG KONG
It seemed ages since we embarked and
there had been nothing but water and
more water around us for days. Our only
companions, other than those on board，
had been occasionally one or two sea-gulls.
The atmosphere was salty and still, in the
setting sun. It was simply awful to be so
At last, in the various shades of or-
ange of the setting sun, we spotted what
we had been longing for during the past
few days- a glimpse of the island which
had been our home for more than
years. Over the horizon arose a patch of
old barren rocks, glistening and glittering in
the gloaming.
As our snip pulea the distance short-
er, the speck
of land grew
arger and
larger until finally it loomed in the water
beyond. A sailor hoisted an English flag
at the bow and the skipper announced over
the loudspeaker that we were approaching
Hong Kong- the Pearl of the Orient.
Atter passing a tew
smallor islands，
we came to the main island itself. It was on
our left. Green undulating hills and white
sanay bays Lined the eastern end of the
island. The view of the peninsula on the
right was much the same.
The flickering
flares of the setting sun made the scenery
of the shore and remote villages even more
peaceful, poetic and romantic.
Char Wan suipped quletly by our lett
as our ship headed for Leymond Pass
the pass to the centre of the bustling
Colony. There was much land along the
shores
reclaimed from
the sea and new
modern estates were built replacing the old
forgotten fishing village.
A magnificent view presented itself as
our ship nosed her way into the
water
beyond the Pass.
In the distant light was
Victoria Harbour, so splendid and impos-
ing, while the dark green hills and the
gereyish orange sky formed the background.
We passed a collection of drab dreary
Olocks on our left, Which we guessed was
Shaukiwan, and came to a dockyard ーa
sign. of the nighly, developed shipping in-
dustry. On our right, we found several en-
ormous gasometers and numerous factory-
hike bulldings — again, symbols of the
booming manufacturing industries of Hong
Kong
Further right, protruding into
Kow-
Loon Bay, lay the new runway of Kai Tak
Airport. A few seawashed boulders marked
its terminal. We were lucky enough to be
able to watch an aeroplane coming in and
touching down, rignt over our heads.
It
was just great and no doubt our ears would
agree that the noise was great too.
In the faint drone of the aeroplane we
crept past a highly urbanized area on our
right and found ourselves side by side with
a typhoon-shelter. 1o our amazement, we
found a patcn of green Clearing behind the
shelter instead of the crowded match boxes.
This we supposed to be Victoria Park.
Entering
into Victoria Harbour we
were greeted by the two densely populated
coasts on both sides. Hung Hum was on
our right while Wan Chai was on our left，
with the unfinished land reclamation pro-
ject and the unfinished flyover to indicate
its position.
We glided past the Naval Dockyard
and came to the centre of the Colon The
Central District and Tsim Sha Tsui.
tall City Hall building，
rising gracetully
Into the twllgnt mist, and the plush hotels
made the place more important looking.
By this time, the sun had glimmered
its last glint and darkness began to creep
over the city. The dark, shabby, weather-
beaten buildings of the railway-station of-
fered a great contrast with the colourful
neon-lights of the Ocean Terminal.
Our ship, was then guided alongside
the Terminal by a tug boat.
Staring into
the utter darkness in front of us, we could
still make out the outlines of the western
side of the Colony— mysterious, peaceful
and quiet, yet we knew that a great deal
of activity was going on in those dimly lit
districts.
A long siren blast of our ship
marked the end of our voyage and I must
say that the striking scenery of Hong Kong
Harbour was extremely enjoyable, enougn
to compensate for the loneliness we suf-
fered in the beginning of our voyage.
Jerome Cheung

147.t: The School Chapel
People never realise how much certain
things mean to them until these are lost.
Seven years have slipped by silently and
just when I am about to leave Wah Yan, I
suddenly appreciate how very attached I am
to it. I shall miss the lawn I have treaded
on many-a-time when Unnoticed, the gold-
fish in the pond which I liked to feel strug-
gling and bouncing in my hands, and even
the endless slope I used to curse. But most
of all, I miss the school chapel.
It is dusky within the chapel.On en-
tering, the first thing that meets my eyes is
the Colossal cross, on which the dying Jesus
welcomes everyone with extended arms.
Below the cross is the barely-adorned altar，
which is significant for its simplicity. But
the most impressive things are the pathetic
Stations of the Cross on the lateral walls.
They manifest vividly the sufferings Our
Lord underwent.
His lean and weary tace
depicts His agony, not so much His phy-
Sical suffering, but the mental wounds in
the depth of His Sacred Heart. Beside Him
are the merciless soldiers who whip and
mock the vulnerable and submissive victim.
I can almost see His lips tremble, His
fragile body dragging the ponderous cross
with the heavier end on the ground, which
makes it even more burdensome for the
over-exhausted Jesus. And there is Mary，
His loving mother, apparently oroken-neart-
ed and helpless. It is obvious that her
mental pain is unparelleled.
Every time, when I enter the chapel
alone, the “Tabernacle lamp' fascinates me.
It shines meekly through the duskiness, and
guides me to the altar like the beam from
a lighthouse. On approaching it, I always
visualize that Our Lord is at the same time
treading softly to meet me, ready to allevi-
ate my troubles and sorrow. It is during
this private rendezvous that I pour forth my
wishes, offer the pains inflicted by others，
and beg Him for the grace St. Francis of
Assisi prayed for，
Grant that I may not so much seek to
be consoled as to console，
To be understood as to understand，
To be loved as to love.
For it is in giving that we receive，
It is in pardoning that We are pardoned，
And it is in dying that we are born to
eternal life.'
and I always emerge from the chapel with
a lighter heart.
Iam glad that our chapel is small. It
provides an atmosphere of intimacy.Dur-
ing Mass, by being near to the priest at the
altar, I feel that I am not watching the
celebration only, I am making the same
offering to God together with the celebrant.
I am no longer an individual but rather, a
part of a closely-united congregation. The
usual lack of communication has vanished.
When the priest says let us offer each other
the sign of peace'， I nod to my neighbours
whole-heartedly, and am completely tree
from the embarrassment often experienced
in other Churches.
The chapel is the most alluring place
in the school.
Yet there is always the
same and small congregation and we al-
ways have the same few Epistle readers.
The organ is cbsolete and seldom played, as
if it is a symbol of the students'
religious
lethargy.There are nearly four hundred
Catholics among us, yet why is it so very
difficult to fill the chapel with pews for two
hundred and fifty？
Louis Au Yeung
（Upper 6 Arts）

148.t: NOISE
The world is changing and making pro-
gress everyday. People are racking their
Orains to try to make their lives more en-
joyable and comfortable. As a result, they
have built great buildings to house them-
selves
in；
they
have
invented
motor
vehicles to save them from walking, and so
on. Parallel with all these modern inven-
tons and progress, though
generally un-
realized and negrectea, 1s the fact that the
present world is not so quiet and peaceful
as it was
when our ancestors
were still
hunting with their slings and clubs.
You wake up In the morning and al-
ready the cicadas are chirping away with
their loudest ‘songs'. You manage to: swal-
low down some breakfast under such ‘ad-
verse'
conditions, stamble down the stairs
and hop onto a bus with the hope of es-
caping from those horrid little creatures and
their irritating tunes.
The whining engine starts and you are
congratulating yourself
on making
the
great escape so successfully.
In a minute
Or two, your bus enters the city district and
you feel that you have congratulated your-
self al, too soon. All the way down town，
you are“entertained' by the hooting cars，
reving
'engines, screeching brakes and the
rush of tyres on the road.
Retreating into your office, you are
greeted with the clatter of typewriters and
the buzz of conversation. Sometimes you
may wonder how an office can be so terri-
fyingly noisy. The telephones
may ring
maddeningly, creating so painful an as-
sault on your eararums that you realy
wish that you were deaf.
A school is much worse the general
hubbub in the classrooms, the clamour of
schoolboys in the playground, the deafen-
ing, unexpected Shouts from the teacher-
all work hard to drive you out of your
mind
You take a walk in the street and
there are the loud appeals of hawkers and
vendors, the earsplitting din of factories，
blending with the hit songs from record
Shops and juke boxes in coffee houses. The
noise of hammering and drilling, the whine
of machinery and the shouts of men com-
ing from construction projects or road work
Will make the strain more unbearable.
Returning home your mind is refreshed
by another collection of noises of a differ-
ent type and nature. The radio or gramo-
phone blares, the children scream and the
people shout.
There is also that horrible
noise coming from a mah-jong table. By
mid-night, these have ceased and then you
think you are going to have a good nap
after all.
Instead, you are awoken in the
middle of the night by a whimpering baby
or by a chorus of barking from a band of
dogs.
You return to your unfinished dreams，
finish your nap and then you have to pre-
pare yourself for the inevitable sufferings
that are to come on the next day.

pletely?This statement suited St. Paul, and

forts. Every now and then, they ask tor
